topic.title: What if the Strait of Hormuz closed?

title: Hormuz shuts for a week. Who runs out first?
description:
The Strait of Hormuz shuts for a week: which country runs out first?
The Strait of Hormuz, the gap of sea between Iran and Oman, and the countries behind it, day by day on the map.
Sources: US Energy Information Administration (Mar 2026). The characters are not advisers.
Maps simplified. Borders as recognised by the country each video is about.
cta: Hormuz or Malacca: which strait should we shut next? Comment

lines.text: The Strait of Hormuz shuts for a week. Which country runs out first?
Every day, about 20.9M barrels of oil sail through this one gap, a lane of sea between Iran's mountains and the tip of Oman.
Day one: the tankers stop. Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain are stuck behind the gate, and their ships have nowhere else to go.
Look at the map: every bit of their coast lies inside the Gulf, like a room with only one door.
Day two: Saudi Arabia has a way round, a pipeline west across the desert to the Red Sea.
Day three: the Emirates pipe oil to Fujairah, a port just outside the strait.
But those two pipes carry only a small part of what the tankers did, and the rest has nowhere to go.
Day four: no new tankers leave for China, India, Japan or South Korea, and most of the oil through Hormuz sails east to Asia.
And the strangest part? Iran ships most of its own oil from inside the Gulf too, from an island called Kharg.
So who runs out first? Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain run out of ways to sell their oil: this gap is their only road out, and it carries about 20% of all the oil the world uses.
Hormuz or Malacca: which strait should we shut next? Tell me below, while the Strait of Hormuz shuts for a week.

payoff: 'Kuwait, Iraq, Qatar and Bahrain have no other way out' is false for Iraq: the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline to Turkey's Mediterranean port is exporting again (restarted 17 Nov 2026 at ~120,000 b/d, aiming at 500,000; 1.5M b/d capacity; Reuters via The National, BOE Report, 17 Nov 2026). Drop Iraq from the 'no way out' list or say Iraq has only a small northern pipe; same for day1's 'stuck behind the gate' if it implies no exit.

payoff/title: 'Who runs out first? The sellers' is a conclusion no source supports: the sellers do not run out of oil, and nothing in the video shows they are hit first (Asian importers hold reserves). Either say what they run out of (a way to sell / storage space / income) and attribute it, or reframe the question so the answer is what the sources show (Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain: no route out but the strait).

day4: 'Day four: tankers for China, India, Japan and South Korea never arrive' is wrong on timing: a tanker from Hormuz takes about 2-3 weeks to East Asia, so ships already at sea still arrive on day four; say instead that no new tankers leave for Asia (EIA: China, India, Japan, South Korea took 74% of Hormuz crude in 1H25, 89% went to Asia, so 'most sails east to Asia' is right).

Confirmed (passes): fact1 20.9M b/d and fact2 about 20% of global petroleum liquids consumption, 1H25, both on the EIA World Oil Transit Chokepoints page (updated 3 Mar 2026). Saudi East-West to Red Sea and UAE pipe to Fujairah exist; EIA: about 4.7M b/d bypass capacity vs 20.9M, so 'only a small part' is fair. Iran: Goreh-Jask effective ~0.3M b/d, so 'most from inside the Gulf' holds. Description ends with the channel disclaimer.
